title: Peeking at A/B test results daily and stopping at p<0.05
content: Question: "What goes wrong if you check A/B results every day and stop when p is below 0.05?" Strong answer: repeated peeking inflates the false-positive (Type I) rate; fixes are a pre-registered fixed horizon with sample size from power analysis, or sequential testing / alpha-spending methods. Related questions in the same set: what is power and what drives it (sample size, effect size, variance, alpha); you tested 20 metrics and one is significant (multiple comparisons: Bonferroni, FDR); when would you NOT run an A/B test (low traffic, network effects, ethics); Simpson's paradox. Geochem angle: relate to multiple-testing when screening many element/isotope variables.

title: Classifier with 98% accuracy on fraud data / imbalanced classes and leakage
content: Question: "Your classifier has 98% accuracy on fraud data. Is it good?" Strong answer: ask about class balance first (a majority-class baseline may already score ~98%), then use precision, recall, PR-AUC, confusion matrix, threshold tuning tied to cost of each error type, class weights/resampling, stratified CV. Companion questions: What is data leakage and how have you caught it (features unavailable at prediction time, time-based split violations); L1 vs L2 regularization (L1 sparsity/feature selection, L2 smooth shrinkage); random forest (bagging) vs gradient boosting (sequential residual correction); how would you detect a deployed model degrading (input/prediction drift, delayed labels, retraining plan). For a geoscientist: leakage via spatial autocorrelation between train/test samples (use spatial/grouped CV) is a good example.

title: Product case: WAU dropped 10% - how do you investigate? (+ SQL retention query)
content: Case/SQL round items: "Weekly active users dropped 10%. How do you investigate?" Strong answer: check data quality/instrumentation/logging first, then segment by platform, region, user type, cohort, then look at releases/seasonality/external events; state hypotheses before computing. Also: write 7-day retention by signup cohort (define 'retained' first; date joins and conditional aggregation); second-highest salary per department (DENSE_RANK, tie handling); rolling 7-day average per user in pandas (sort, groupby + rolling); measure success of a recommendation feature (one primary metric, guardrails, novelty effect). Typical loop: recruiter screen, SQL/Python technical screen, stats & experiments, ML, case, behavioral, sometimes take-home.

title: Core stats conceptual set: central tendency, correlation, outliers, hypothesis test, CI, CLT
content: Exponent/Aced guide (compiled from real candidate questions; input from Amazon, Google, Tinder, BCG, Instacart DS). Stats round has numerical, conceptual and applied question types. Examples: mean vs median in positively skewed data (mean larger, outlier-sensitive); interpret correlation of +0.8 (linear, standardized; not causation; note the guide's '80% of increase' phrasing is loose - be precise, r^2=0.64); detect outliers (1.5xIQR rule, z-score); design a hypothesis test (hypotheses, test choice, alpha, statistic, critical region/p-value, interpretation); define p-value; Type I vs II; CLT and why it underpins tests; correct interpretation of 95% confidence interval (frequentist repeated-sampling meaning). Also a Tinder DS question: determine sample size for an experiment. Practice explaining each in plain words then with math.

title: FanDuel: design an ML monitoring system for a fantasy sports app
content: Asked at FanDuel: "How would you design an ML monitoring system for a fantasy sports app, taking into account outliers, data quality, and drift?" Strong answer covers: input data validation (schema, missingness, range checks), outlier detection (IQR/z-score) on features, feature/prediction drift metrics (PSI, KS test), concept drift detection with delayed labels, performance dashboards and alert thresholds, retraining triggers and rollback. Analogy for a geochemist: instrument drift/QC standards in analytical labs.

title: Academia-to-industry transition questions (Insight Data Science style)
content: Typical PhD-transition questions (Insight Data Science guide): Why do you want to move from academia to data science? Professional goals for next 2-5 years? Which sectors interest you? Explain your complex PhD research to a non-technical person (e.g. your grandmother). Also commonly asked there: statistical significance in hypothesis testing, design an experiment for a product change (hard, very common), validate an ML model, purpose of cross-validation, bias-variance tradeoff, handling messy datasets. Prepare a 2-min non-jargon geochemistry story framed as problem -> data -> method -> decision/impact, plus a quantitative example of messy data handling (detection limits, missing values, batch effects).

title: Interview Query: frequency of DS interview topics (SQL >90%, ML 85%, Python 80%)
content: Interview Query's 110-question guide reports SQL asked in over 90% of data science interviews, machine learning 85%+, Python 80%+, plus statistics/A-B testing and data structures & algorithms. Use it to prioritize: a PhD with strong stats but weaker SQL should spend early prep time on SQL (joins, window functions, aggregation). Sample questions listed: predict customer churn, A/B test significance, feature importance analysis, clean missing data, neural network architecture, Bayesian probability, recommend similar products. Also useful: GitHub repo youssefHosni/Data-Science-Interview-Questions-Answers (ML Q&A on outlier robustness, bias-variance, imbalance, SVM scaling, concept vs data drift).

title: Entry-level ML interview set: normalization, dimensionality reduction, EDA, model choice, CNN theory
content: Written by a master's-level grad who interviewed for entry-level DS/ML/NLP/CV roles at Amazon, Tesla, Samsung, Uber, Huawei and startups. Questions asked: why normalize data (equal feature weighting in the loss, better convergence); explain dimensionality reduction and its benefits (storage, speed, redundancy removal, visualization, less overfitting); handle missing/corrupted data (drop vs impute; pandas isnull/dropna/fillna); explain a clustering algorithm; how to do EDA (coarse-to-fine: df.info, class imbalance, distributions, pairwise plots, PCA, then start with simple baselines like linear regression/Naive Bayes before SVM/trees/NN, check ROC/precision/recall); how to choose a model (no free lunch); handle imbalanced data; for CV roles: why convolutions vs FC layers, translation invariance, max-pooling, residual nets, batch norm, small 3x3 kernels. Closing questions were project-based: 'explain your current research - what worked, what didn't, future directions?' A strong answer for a geochemist: prepare an EDA walkthrough using a geochemical dataset (compositional data, missing values below detection limit) and a research explanation with failures and next steps.

title: Presenting PhD research in a 20-minute verbal industry interview (5-part structure)
content: From a CS PhD student's account of PhD research-internship interviews (Google, Meta AI, Salesforce, Adobe, Pinterest, etc.). Research interviews usually took ~20 minutes or less; some companies asked candidates to present a paper they did NOT author. Slides usually weren't needed unless the recruiter emailed otherwise. Suggested structure: (1) general problem, (2) how people currently solve it and shortcomings, (3) your solution in one sentence, (4) significance in one sentence, (5) then details: method, experimental setup, results. Keep it brief, use short sentences, leave room for the interviewer to interrupt so it becomes a discussion. Prep tips from the same source: re-implement basic ML algorithms from scratch, refresh bias-variance, SVM, precision/recall, AUC; practice DS&A (Blind 75/NeetCode) for companies that ask it; referrals helped get past resume screens; big tech intern interviews often start in Dec or later. Geochemist action: draft a 5-part version of your thesis using non-geoscience vocabulary and also prepare a paper-walkthrough of someone else's ML paper.

title: Microsoft Data & Applied Scientist PhD intern interview format (Blind thread)
content: Blind thread (Feb 2021) from a PhD grad facing a Microsoft Data & Applied Scientist intern interview: recruiter said 4 rounds of 60 min. A former D&AS PhD intern (summer 2019) reported four ~45-min rounds covering: (1) ML algorithms and performance metrics, (2) experimental design, (3) open-ended case studies, (4) more structured/linear case studies; no coding rounds for them, though other product areas had a coding round. Team isn't always known in advance; each team hires independently. Another commenter: applied ML team -> recap ML basics; analytical DS team -> recap SQL; the last round may be with the hiring manager with more design/abstract questions. Intern rigor equals full-time because most interns convert. Prep: ML algorithms + metrics, A/B/experimental design, open-ended case reasoning, SQL refresher, and ask the recruiter which team/product area. Note: 2021 anecdotal data, so confirm current format.

title: GitHub: 36 core ML interview Q&As (regularization, boosting vs RF, PCA, drift, ARIMA)
content: Free resource: youssefHosni's 'Machine Learning Interview Questions & Answers for Data Scientists' (36 questions; repo also has Statistics, Probability, Python, SQL, Deep Learning files). Highest-yield for new-grad PhD screens: L1 vs L2 regularization; bias-variance; random forest vs gradient boosting; handling outliers and missing data; logistic regression; batch/SGD/mini-batch GD; entropy/information gain; linear regression assumptions; choosing K in K-Means; precision/recall/F1 trade-off; MSE vs MAE loss; parametric vs non-parametric; kernel trick; cross-validation; imbalanced data; ROC; curse of dimensionality and PCA variants; scaling for SVM; concept vs data drift; ARIMA assumptions (relevant to geoscience time series). Use as a self-quiz: answer aloud in ~60-90 seconds each, with a concrete example from your geochemical data (e.g. regularization for many correlated element concentrations, PCA for compositional data).

title: DoorDash new-grad DS/ML loop: take-home + ML round + 2 'business intuition' A/B rounds
content: Blind account (Feb 2021) from a new-grad (master's) DoorDash DS/ML candidate: the process began with a take-home advertised as 6 hours that took ~20 hours; then a virtual onsite with 1 ML round and 2 'business intuition' rounds. ML round drew on methods from coursework and DoorDash/Lyft/Uber Eats engineering blogs (candidate spent ~60 hours reading them). Business-intuition rounds asked very specific A/B testing scenarios with made-up metrics (non-standard experiment design), which a candidate without experiment experience struggled with. Commenters advise: A/B testing questions are standard at Bay Area tech DS roles; read 'Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments' (Kohavi); study company case studies/engineering blogs; practise communicating business implications; note that 2 product-sense rounds signal an experimentation-heavy analytics DS role rather than a pure ML role. Prep for a geochemist: learn randomization, sample size/power, metric choice, interference/network effects, and how to reason about guardrail metrics even without industry experience. Anecdotal, 2021.

title: Four-hour plan for a time-boxed DS take-home (SQLPad)
content: SQLPad guide (updated Oct 2026) with a 240-minute schedule: 0-20 scope the brief/assumptions; 20-65 inspect and validate data (row meaning, key uniqueness, units, missingness, join cardinality; keep raw data unchanged; log exclusions); 65-140 core answer with a simple baseline; 140-180 one sensitivity/validation check; 180-220 write report (recommendation first, then evidence, limitations); 220-240 clean-run and packaging. Key rubric points: don't mean-impute everything; fit preprocessing on training data only (leakage); validation split should resemble deployment (time-based split for forecasts, group split for repeated subjects such as samples from the same site/core); pick a decision-tied primary metric plus a segment failure check; keep test set out of model selection; separate prediction from causation (feature importance != causes); put extras in an appendix; README + reproducible run order; no employer data in public repos or external AI tools. Be ready to defend your baseline, one rejected alternative and the next check. Geochemist angle: spatial/group CV for samples from the same site is a natural talking point.

title: Amazon Applied Scientist intern: official OA + loop structure (Aug 2026 guide)
content: PracHub guide (Aug 21, 2026) summarizing Amazon's official student page: Applied Science Intern OA = ~70 min coding (Python/R etc. allowed; browser use logged, public docs only) + a work-styles assessment (not an ML quiz; answer consistently). Then 1-2 technical screens and a ~4 interview loop (problem solving/coding, ML depth & breadth, research/tech talk, Leadership Principles). Coding target: medium DSA (arrays, strings, hash maps, sorting, binary search, heaps, trees, graphs, intervals, basic DP). Strong answer: restate, ask constraints, baseline then improve, state complexity, test edge cases, talk aloud. ML breadth/depth topics: linear/logistic regression, trees/ensembles, bias-variance, regularization, calibration, class imbalance, cross-validation, Bayes rule, CIs, hypothesis testing, sampling bias, experiment design, choosing metrics by cost structure (precision-recall, temporal splits), plus transformers/CNNs/recsys per resume. Includes a 7-day prep plan ending with a full simulation (coding + ML depth + behavioral).

title: Amazon AS: PhD research deep-dive and "why that architecture" questions (Glassdoor, Sep 2026)
content: Recent Glassdoor reports (Sep 2026): one accepted-offer candidate (Seattle) described a sequence of ML questions, LeetCode, Leadership Principles, situational cases ("what would you do solving this problem") and questions about their PhD research. Another (screen, Apr 2026) got basic AI/ML + project questions focused on justifying choices, e.g. "why did you pick that architecture?". Another process: recruiter prep call, initial coding assessment, then 5 loop interviews. Prep: a 2-minute plain-language pitch of your thesis, be able to defend every modeling choice (alternatives, ablations, trade-offs), prepare 6-8 STAR stories mapped to Leadership Principles, and practice LeetCode medium. For a geochemist: frame thesis as problem -> data -> method -> validation -> impact.

title: Amazon Applied Scientist ML breadth round: tree/RF/dropout/overfitting questions
content: GeeksforGeeks write-up (campus new-grad loop Oct 2023, page updated Jul 2025). 5 rounds: DSA+resume, ML breadth, ML depth, scalable ML, ML applications/managerial. Coding: largest lexicographic substring ("ababaa" -> "babaa"); reverse linked list in groups of K (40-45 min; interviewer gave hints - talk aloud). Resume probe: metrics, loss function, why that model over others, impact on business metrics. ML breadth questions: explain decision tree and random forest; why RF beats a single tree (many deep high-variance trees, decorrelated via row/feature subsampling -> variance reduction); what is regularization and is dropout one (and derive/write equation); how dropout weights are handled at inference; when to scale inputs for NNs; given two models' fit()/eval() and new test data, how to decide which is better and which overfits (compare train vs held-out, CV, not just train-low/test-high); K-means. Candidate was rejected - lesson: need both breadth and mathematical depth, plus Leadership Principles.

title: Motive Applied Scientist 1: ML coding on two CSVs + ML theory + scenario questions (Nov 2025)
content: GeeksforGeeks report (Nov 2025), Motive Applied Scientist 1, no LeetCode. Process: hackathon -> resume shortlist -> (1) 90-min ML coding: given two CSVs with different attributes of same entity, build a classifier (merge, dedupe, feature select, encode categoricals, logistic regression + random forest); follow-ups: why RF performs well, what happens if duplicates not removed (leakage/overfitting), what to improve (sklearn pipelines). (2) 90-min ML theory: thesis questions (IMU sensors, odometry), precision/recall and PR curve axes/area/threshold choice, regularization for trees/RF, LLM vs LSTM advantages, explain LLM architecture layer by layer, class weighting to prioritize one class, AdaBoost and adapting it, scenario questions (new PM requirement, multi-stakeholder story, external AI API with sensitive data -> mask/anonymize then build in-house model). (3) 'Top grading' deep dive on projects: model choice, fine-tuning, knowledge distillation. Good practice for a PhD with domain thesis: be ready to explain your thesis domain to ML interviewers.

title: Amazon Applied Scientist ML-coding question list (PracHub, updated 2026)
content: PracHub's Amazon Applied Scientist page (updated May-Aug 2026; 80 candidate-reported questions, some tagged New Grad, many Senior+ so filter) lists question titles worth practicing: implement K-means (+interval/frequency tasks); implement multi-head attention from scratch in NumPy; implement top-p (nucleus) sampling in NumPy; implement a PyTorch training loop; derive mean and variance via maximum likelihood; merge overlapping time ranges; course schedule (cycle detection in directed graph); two-sum; binary search lower/upper bound; shortest path in grid with obstacles; optimal bucket batching; evolution of NLP embeddings to LLM embeddings; design RAG end-to-end (skip S3 design as senior-level). Page describes loop as recruiter + tech phone screen, then 4-6 rounds mixing ML depth, ML breadth, coding, and Leadership Principles/Bar Raiser. Note: site is a paid platform; solutions partly locked - use titles as a checklist.

title: Microsoft Applied Scientist (AS1/AS2) process: 30-min ML-grounded phone screen + design rounds (2026)
content: Aced/Exponent guide (updated ~Oct 2026). Microsoft hires AS1 (entry) and AS2 (PhD, or MS + ~2 yrs). Flow: recruiter screen (30 min, team fit, technical credibility on your own work) -> 30-min technical phone screen with one interviewer: ~15 min ML-grounded coding (example reported: top-n most frequent words from a list of sentences), ~5 min CV/projects, 5-10 min ML fundamentals -> onsite panel of 3-5: hiring-manager round (ML depth/breadth, probes every CV project until gaps show, feedback/growth mindset), two end-to-end ML pipeline design rounds (data collection, preprocessing, model choice, eval, production; narrate trade-offs), optional extra coding round. Calibration is by team leaders, not an Amazon-style bar raiser. Key advice: explain models at the building-block level (mechanics, not buzzwords); Microsoft moved away from pure algorithmic puzzles for this screen.

title: Microsoft Data & Applied Scientist: Codility test (pandas + lasso/ridge/elastic net), kth largest (Apr-Jun 2024)
content: Glassdoor reports (Apr-Jun 2024), Microsoft Data and Applied Scientist. One candidate: ~2.5-hour Codility test with (1) a lengthy pandas data-manipulation task on a phone-company-style database and (2) a task on lasso, ridge and elastic net; then resume screening and a live coding round. Another: first round = 30 min technical questions from resume, then ~25 min coding (find the kth largest number - use heap/quickselect, discuss complexity). Accepted-offer Bengaluru report: 5 rounds - two DS rounds with a DS coding question, DS design round, one DSA round, hiring manager round, optional ML/coding round; topics ML basics, project walkthrough, DSA. Prep: pandas groupby/merge fluency, implement/compare L1 vs L2 vs elastic net (sparsity, correlated features, when to use), heaps/kth-largest.

title: Amazon unfair-coin to fair bits (von Neumann), study-bias, fraud-model metric questions (Dec 2025)
content: Dataloopr (Dec 11, 2025) collects Amazon/Tesla DS-style questions that also appear in Amazon applied-scientist screens (IGotAnOffer lists the unfair-coin item under Amazon coding/modeling; an AS intern reported a Bayesian coin-toss problem in a peer-coding screen). (1) Given a biased coin (p != 0.5), generate unbiased 0/1: von Neumann extractor - flip twice, HT->1, TH->0, discard HH/TT; works since P(HT)=P(TH)=p(1-p); expected pairs per bit = 1/(2p(1-p)), inefficient for extreme p; be able to code it. (2) Bias in a study claiming an airline has fastest boarding: selection bias, sample size, time of day, aircraft size, demographics, measurement definition, self-reported data; propose stratified analysis and significance testing. (3) Fraud-detection model with SMS confirmation: supervised binary classification (LR/RF/GBT, anomaly detection if labels sparse), class imbalance, real-time scoring, trade-off of false positives (annoyed customers) vs false negatives (loss); choose precision/recall/PR-AUC by cost, not accuracy. Also related: simulate a fair die from a biased coin, expected tosses to see HTH.

title: SQL screen staples: second-highest salary (DENSE_RANK vs LIMIT/OFFSET) and finding duplicate emails
content: Dataquest guide (Oct 30, 2026) lists 31 DS questions by round; the SQL screen is typically in a shared online editor. Q1: 'Given an employees table with tied salaries, return the second-highest salary.' Strong answer: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) in a subquery (WHERE runs before window functions) and SELECT DISTINCT; explain why plain LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 fails with ties (skips a row, not a salary) - fix with DISTINCT; generalize to Nth-highest; handle no-such-salary case by wrapping to return NULL. Q2: 'Find emails that appear more than once in users table.' Strong answer: GROUP BY LOWER(email) HAVING COUNT(*)>1 (HAVING not WHERE because filtering after aggregation; normalize case or you miss KIM@example.com); follow-up: which duplicate to keep (oldest/most recent). The guide maps rounds: SQL screen, stats/experiments, ML, Python (pandas bucket counts by grade, small functions like palindrome check with regex), product case, behavioral.

title: Python coding-screen question bank: arrays/strings, Kadane, combinations, sample-from-normal histogram, apply vs applymap
content: GitHub repo (youssefHosni) Python list for DS interviews, 15 questions. Typical asks: (1) intersection of two arrays (use sets); (2) find duplicates in an array (seen-set pass, O(n)); (3) max product of three numbers (consider two negatives - compare top3 product vs two smallest x largest); (4) max contiguous subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm, O(n)); (5) tuples vs lists (mutability, memory); (6) Euclidean distance between two Series via numpy; (7) k-combinations of 1..n (itertools.combinations or recursion/backtracking); (8) generate N samples from a normal distribution and plot histogram (np.random.normal + plt.hist, mention seed and doing it from scratch via Box-Muller); (9) apply vs applymap (elementwise on DataFrame vs row/column-wise; note applymap is now DataFrame.map in newer pandas); (10) first recurring character (use set, not repeated .count which is O(n^2)); (11) recursive factorial with edge cases (negative returns -1); (12) longest increasing path in a matrix (DFS + memoization); (13) Flask; (15) ways to handle missing data. Strong answers state time/space complexity and edge cases, and prefer set/hash-map solutions. Good for a PhD without CS background to rehearse; date of repo undetermined (reference resource).

title: Microsoft Applied Science PhD Intern (Redmond, Feb 2026): ablation, precision/recall coding, RAG design
content: FastPrep report 006 (Feb 2026): one screen then three back-to-back interviews; offer received. Topics: project + ablation-study discussion, NLP/ML fundamentals, RL/agents/metrics/regularization. Coding: (1) given [-1,-2,-4,-5,7,10] return every pair with the minimum difference (easy; sort + adjacent scan); (2) 10 animal images, API returns k files, compute precision and recall for 'dog' and handle edge cases like None or result count != k; (3) design a RAG system (agentic tool framing). Strong answer: justify ablations (what you removed and why), robust input validation, define precision/recall explicitly, and discuss RAG retrieval/eval/failure modes.

title: Microsoft Applied Scientist Intern (Feb 2026): K-means from scratch, hypothesis testing, Python debug, case study
content: FastPrep report 007 (Feb 2026): phone screen on ML and LLM fundamentals, then three virtual-onsite rounds; offer. Questions: implement K-means from scratch and discuss time complexity (O(n·k·d·iterations)); business hypothesis-testing question; simple Python debugging; project discussion; open-ended case study. Related PhD intern reports from the same page: implement a precision-recall curve (Data Scientist PhD intern, Jan 2026; also KNN, PCA, LLM fundamentals), design counterfactual evaluation when A/B testing is unavailable, diagnose a sudden one-day product-metric drop, 'explain how ChatGPT is trained' (Oct 2025). Prepare to code basic ML algorithms in numpy without libraries and reason about experiments.

title: AI research internship hunt as PhD student: process, prep list, 20-min research talk format (Mar 2024)
content: Substack post by a 3rd-year CS PhD (Mar 2024) covering interviews at Google, Meta, Adobe, Salesforce, Pinterest, etc. Process: OA/take-home (ML/DL or DS&A coding, sometimes ML MCQs) -> technical interviews (LeetCode-style or ML coding, LLM/DL questions, research presentation) -> hiring-manager behavioral. Prep: Blind 75 / NeetCode 150; reimplement basic ML algorithms; refresh bias-variance, SVM, precision/recall, AUC; read 'Attention is All You Need' and HF docs for GenAI roles. Research talk template (~20 min, verbal, leave room for Q&A): problem -> existing approaches and shortcomings -> your solution in one sentence -> significance in one sentence -> details/setup/results. Some companies ask you to present a paper you did not author. Useful for a geochem PhD translating research into an ML-audience talk. Timing note: startups open early fall, big tech later; referrals helped pass resume screen.

title: Amazon/AWS Applied Scientist virtual onsite (PhD): 40-min research talk + ML depth/breadth/open-ended (Blind, Feb 2022)
content: Blind thread (Feb 2022, older but loop format still echoed in 2026 reports): successful candidate's virtual onsite = 40-min presentation of own research + 15 min Q&A (clear visuals, leave >=10 min at end since time management is assessed, tie to customer impact); 2 coding rounds (algorithms/DS); ML depth (interviewer probes your talk, e.g. 'why is there a normalization layer there?', often open-ended asking for plausible scientific reasoning); ML breadth (rapid-fire list of classic + DL questions, not limited to your subfield; you aren't expected to know everything); ML open-ended (hiring manager gives an Amazon-style problem to scope and propose solutions). All 5 interviews start with ~half behavioral (Leadership Principles) so prepare many STAR stories. For a geochem PhD: build the talk so a non-domain ML audience follows it, and be ready to defend every modeling choice.

title: PracHub DS statistics bank: topics + sample questions (updated Sep 2026)
content: PracHub's Data Scientist Statistics & Math bank (507 questions, updated 30 Sep 2026; Meta, Google, Uber, Capital One, Citadel, Waymo). Reported question themes: justify why comment-count data is right-skewed not normal (pick the distribution and defend it); probability of a 4th good response after three successes; who is missing from a survey sample (sampling bias); what a p-value does and does not tell you; regularisation, resampling, and metrics for imbalanced classifiers. Sample items: 'Explain p-values and confidence intervals in simple linear regression' (Google, Sep 2026); 'Compare two rare-event rates with different exposure' (Waymo, Sep 2026; Poisson rates with exposure/offset, rate-ratio test); 'Measure bird species segregation' (an ecology-flavored stats question, relevant to a natural-science PhD). Strong answers state assumptions, name the distribution/test, and interpret in plain language. Statistics is graded verbally (no code), so rehearse explaining out loud. Note some solutions are paywalled.

title: Probability screen staples: coin/disease Bayes, HH vs TH, expected rolls, ants, MLE of exponential
content: Nick Singh (DataLemur) list of 40 probability/stats questions tagged by company. Probability examples: fair vs two-tailed coin, 5 tails in a row, P(unfair) (Facebook, Bayes); HH vs TH coin game (Lyft); disease 1/1000 with 98% sensitivity & 1% false-positive, P(disease | positive) (Amazon); expected rolls to see all 6 faces (Facebook); expected flips to get HH (Two Sigma); three ants on triangle no collision (Bloomberg); fair odds from biased coin (Airbnb); A with n+1 coins vs B with n coins (Robinhood). Stats examples: explain a confidence interval to non-technical audience (Facebook), correlated predictors in multiple regression (Two Sigma), p-value in layman's terms (Uber), MLE of lambda for exponential lifetimes (Stripe), derive mean/variance of U(a,b) (Lyft), MLE vs MAP (Uber). Page also lists what to review: counting/combinatorics, expectation/variance/covariance, Uniform/Normal/Poisson/Binomial/Geometric, CLT, p-values, CIs, Type I/II errors, linear regression, MLE, Bayesian stats. Strong answers state the model/distribution, set up the conditioning (Bayes table) and show the derivation. Good fit for a PhD with solid stats background: practise out loud. Note: page date not shown (undated), but content is evergreen fundamentals.

title: Correlation vs causation, Type I/II error, and "8 heads in 10 flips" exact-test question
content: From Interview Pilot's DS guide (updated May 2026). Three easy/medium stats questions with model answers: (1) Correlation vs causation: strong answer names confounding, reverse causality, selection bias, and proposes RCT / natural experiment / IV / RDD / diff-in-diff; example: push notifications and retention; follow-ups: sources of confounding, how to test causality. (2) Type I vs Type II error: false positive vs false negative, alpha vs power (1-beta), sample size trade-off, and tie the acceptable error to cost (risky checkout change vs low-risk UI tweak; medical diagnosis). (3) A coin lands heads 8/10 times - is it biased? Null p=0.5; P(>=8 heads)=56/1024≈5.5%; two-sided ≈10.9%, so not significant at 5%. Also defines p-value (not P(null true)), CI (method coverage over repeated samples), power, selection bias. Useful for a geochemist: practise computing exact binomial tail probabilities by hand and stating interpretations carefully.

title: PracHub DS statistics & math question bank (company-tagged, Sept 2026 update)
content: PracHub's Data Scientist Statistics & Math category: ~500 questions from 81 companies (Meta, Capital One, Google, Uber, Citadel, Waymo), last updated 30 Sep 2026; 81% readable without premium. Themes: explain why a comment-count distribution is right-skewed not normal; probability of a fourth success after three; who is missing from a survey sample (selection bias); what a p-value does/doesn't say; regularisation, resampling, metrics for imbalanced classifiers; Poisson mean/variance; compare two rare-event rates with different exposure (e.g., incidents per mile, Waymo); Google: explain p-values and CIs in simple linear regression. Difficulty spread from easy definitions (116) to hard derivations (88); Capital One leans credit-risk framing, Citadel leans expected value/combinatorics. Use it for targeted practice of stats answered out loud with no code. Caveat: page contains heavy marketing/testimonials; treat claims of 'exact questions' skeptically.

title: Microsoft PhD summer DS intern (Stats PhD): OA + 3 resume-driven rounds, precision-recall curve coding
content: PracHub report (interview Jan 2026, published Aug 2026), offer received. Timeline: HackerRank OA (one LeetCode-style + one data-processing problem) -> three back-to-back rounds -> offer a month later. R1: 30 min behavioral + 15 min ML fundamentals (KNN and PCA), no coding. R2: 35 min deep-dive on resume projects + 20 min coding: compute and plot a precision-recall curve (candidate had to recall definition of recall; practise implementing precision/recall/thresholds from scratch and with sklearn+matplotlib). R3: 15 min resume + 15 min rapid-fire LLM fundamentals. No SQL/LeetCode in the live rounds. Key lesson: nearly every question, including behavioral ones, was pulled back to the research projects, with technical follow-ups; the candidate was weakest on ML fundamentals outside the resume. Prep: be able to explain each project's setup concisely to non-experts, and refresh KNN (tuning k, distance, scaling), PCA, PR vs ROC metrics.

title: Capital One Data Science Intern process: OA, manager call (elementary ML), Power Day
content: Glassdoor reports (Capital One DS Intern, page updated 3 Nov 2026; 2025-26 interviews). Process: online assessment with four Python data-science coding problems (reported very hard / near impossible to finish fully, but partial credit still passed), HR call/background check, then possible wait of ~3 months to be matched to a team, a 30-min hiring-manager call (elementary ML: boosting trees, neural networks, logistic regression; 'tell me about your experience'), then Power Day of 4 consecutive one-hour rounds: coding/role-play round, business-insight (case) round, and manager call on behavior/culture fit. Average difficulty 3.2/5; avg ~39 days to hire. Capital One also lists a Summer 2027 PhD AI Engineering Internship. Prep: timed pandas/Python problem solving with partial solutions, ML fundamentals for boosted trees/NN/logistic regression, and a business-case structure (ties to Capital One-heavy statistics questions in credit-risk framing).

title: Uber Applied Scientist I: stats/experimentation screens (Glassdoor 2026)
content: Uber AS I reports (Mar-Jul 2026): recruiter screen, then tech screen with easy/medium SQL, Python and statistics; one report describes onsite of 5 rounds (coding, business case, stakeholder management, 2 technical on stats/experimentation/ML/NLP). Questions reported: 'How would you reduce variance in control and test groups?' (strong answer: CUPED/covariate adjustment, stratification/blocking, larger N, outlier handling, paired designs); 'When to use synthetic control vs A/B testing vs difference-in-differences?' (know assumptions: randomization feasible, parallel trends, donor pool fit); basic Python/SQL manipulation, writing a simple function. Another earlier report: how to design an A/B test with spillovers (switchback/cluster randomization). Hiring-manager rejection rate reported as high, so prep causal inference thoroughly.

title: Uber Applied Scientist Intern: research chat + 2 coding + metric/case study (2023-24)
content: Uber AS intern reports (Jul 2023-Feb 2024; page last updated Feb 2024, newest available for intern level). Format: (1) resume/research projects discussion with follow-ups on econometric models; (2) two coding questions (e.g., CodeSignal 'compute integer square root' - candidate failed for not being efficient; know binary search/Newton's method); (3) case study covering models and metrics. Case prompts: design a metric for time food is prepared vs rider arrival at restaurant; 'should Uber Eats and Rides be separated?'; (other report) match drivers and riders at an airport. First round also included LeetCode, SQL and A/B testing. Strong answers: define metric precisely, discuss gaming/edge cases, propose model + evaluation, state tradeoffs.

title: Adobe research/applied scientist loop: 60-min PhD-defense-style talk + 4-5 technical 1:1s
content: Adobe Research Scientist reports (Glassdoor, 2025; one interview dated Oct 2023): loop starts with ~60-min research talk incl. Q&A, similar to a PhD defense, followed by 4-5 one-on-one technical interviews of 30-45 min, then hiring manager round; one candidate said it was a full-day in-person process. Technical content: detailed engineering questions from deep generative models and sequence modeling to system design for training models; coding mostly LeetCode medium/hard. Advice from candidates: brush up ML breadth and know deeply anything you claim expertise in. Adobe 2026 new-grad Applied Scientist postings (PhD/MS) ask for gen-AI training, fine-tuning/alignment/distillation, PyTorch. Prepare a talk that a general ML audience can follow and defend each method choice.

title: Zillow Applied Scientist: ML/DL fundamentals, no LeetCode, applied design + seasonality (2024-2026)
content: Zillow AS reports (Glassdoor, Aug 2024-Jul 2026): recruiter/HR call about background, then a hiring-manager/technical round. A Dec 2025 candidate got many ML/DL questions ranging from basic linear regression to transformer attention, no LeetCode, and was given a specific application problem to design a solution/algorithm for. A 2024 candidate was asked 'how to estimate seasonality in the simplest way possible' (decomposition, seasonal dummies/Fourier terms, seasonal averages, STL). Earlier snippet also mentions vision transformers vs CNN, overfitting, multimodal GenAI system design. Prep: linear regression assumptions/derivation, attention mechanics, time-series basics, and structured approach to open-ended applied problems (data, features, model, metric, deployment). Process can be slow (up to 4 months reported).

title: Interview Kickstart Amazon Applied Scientist guide (Apr 2026): levels, rounds, team map
content: Interview Kickstart guide (updated Apr 1, 2026). Useful for orientation: AS I = L4, 0-3 yrs (implements existing ML models, analysis, supports seniors) - the new-grad PhD target. Process: recruiter -> 45-60 min phone screen (ML breadth+depth, explain past projects and modeling decisions, stats, coding/DSA) -> 4-6 round virtual loop (ML, applied scientific thinking, coding, project/tech presentation, behavioral) -> bar raiser. Candidates are matched to teams (AWS, AGI, Alexa, ops/supply chain, retail, ads, trust & store integrity, robotics, sustainability), so research the team. Sample questions it lists: offline-good/online-bad model debugging (leakage, distribution shift, metric misalignment, feedback loops), Adam vs SGD, L1 vs L2, multiple hypothesis testing, A/B test design (novelty effects, noncompliance), K-means implementation, union-find, aggregating a 2GB/50M-row CSV. Skip its system-design/senior sections for entry level.

title: Microsoft Applied Scientist (Apr 2026): 30-min screen + 3 same-day rounds incl. 2D conv coding
content: Glassdoor Microsoft AS reports (Apr-Aug 2026). Boston candidate (Apr 2026): 30-min screen = shallow dive into a resume project + short classification-modeling case study; then three back-to-back 45-min rounds: (1) resume grilling - deep dive into a research project and applications; (2) behavioral with non-conventional questions (how to ask a senior colleague for help, how you use AI tools in work); (3) live coding - implement a 2D convolution operation (practice from-scratch NumPy conv, stride/padding). Redmond candidate: a 30-min screen with self-intro plus 2 easy coding questions on linear regression/basic ML - time pressure, so be concise. Cairo candidate: 4 back-to-back rounds with LeetCode medium (DP, backtracking) plus data science concepts. Overall Glassdoor difficulty 3.3/5.

title: PracHub Applied Scientist New Grad/Intern bank: attention from scratch, MAB simulation, MLE derivation (2026)
content: PracHub's cross-company Applied Scientist bank (104 questions, updated 2026; solutions are paywalled in parts) tags many items as New Grad/Intern. Examples to practice: implement multi-head attention from basic tensor operations and explain dimensions (ByteDance AS intern/new grad, Nov 2026); simulate and compare multi-armed bandit strategies recording reward and regret (AS New Grad, Sep 2026); derive normal-distribution MLE for mean/variance and explain why MLE variance is biased vs unbiased sample variance; optimize BERT inference latency/throughput (ByteDance new grad); extensible card-hand ranking OOP design; Amazon-tagged: bucket batching of document lengths across G GPUs, top-p sampling in NumPy, PyTorch training loop, K-means. Use as a topic checklist; note it is a commercial aggregator whose 'real question' claims can't be independently verified.
